fixes.explanation: Guard duty never comes up, friend. The enemies of Judah and Benjamin walk up to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah (Haggai 1:1), and say, “Let us build with you…” (Ezra 4:2). They're asking for a spot on the crew, not a night shift by the altar. That's a job nobody posted.

Cyrus king of Persia is the one. Zerubbabel and the family heads say they must build “…as Cyrus king of Persia has commanded us.” (Ezra 4:3). Notice they don't just say no. They point to the king's command. That's a firm no with a king's name behind it.

The text says the people of the land “…set out to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to build.” (Ezra 4:4). Their aim is discouragement and fear. I think that kind of pressure can wear a builder down.

Darius king of Persia is the answer. The counselors work against Judah “…throughout the reign of Cyrus king of Persia and down to the reign of Darius king of Persia.” (Ezra 4:5). That's a long stretch of kings, and the counselors are at it through all of it.

Belshazzar is a king from Daniel's book (Daniel 5:1), but he didn't make the roster for this verse. The counselors keep going “…down to the reign of Darius king of Persia.” (Ezra 4:5). The text names two Persian kings here, Cyrus and Darius.

Hebrew is a fair guess, friend, but the text says the letter “…was written in Aramaic and then translated.” (Ezra 4:7). Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel and their associates wrote it to King Artaxerxes. A letter written in one language and then translated is a letter with a layover.

Rehum and Shimshai call Jerusalem “…that rebellious and wicked city.” (Ezra 4:12). That's how they describe it in their letter to the king. Those are their words about the city, and they put them in writing.

Rent never makes it into this letter, friend. Rehum and Shimshai warn the king that “…they will not pay tribute, duty, or toll, and the royal treasury will suffer.” (Ezra 4:13). Tribute, duty and toll are three payments, and the letter has them all headed to the king. Not a landlord in sight.

Nobody suggests asking the priests, friend. Rehum and Shimshai say “…that a search should be made of the record books of your fathers.” (Ezra 4:15). The proof they point to is written in the king's own fathers' records. Priests don't come up in this part of the letter.

The letter doesn't send the king to anything from Cyrus, friend. Rehum and Shimshai say “…that a search should be made of the record books of your fathers.” (Ezra 4:15). Old records are what they name. Cyrus's command (Ezra 4:3) is a different pile of paper.

The letter warns that “…you will have no dominion west of the Euphrates.” (Ezra 4:16). Dominion means the king's rule over that region. That's where Rehum and Shimshai end their warning. It's like closing an email with "URGENT" in capital letters.

Trade isn't in this warning, friend. Rehum and Shimshai write, “…you will have no dominion west of the Euphrates.” (Ezra 4:16). Dominion means rule, so the line is about the king's rule over the region, not commerce.

The king says, “It was discovered that this city has revolted against kings from ancient times, engaging in rebellion and sedition.” (Ezra 4:19). That's what came back after he issued a decree and a search was conducted. Artaxerxes sent folks digging, and that's the report he's holding.

It's true. The king says, “And mighty kings have ruled over Jerusalem and exercised authority over the whole region west of the Euphrates; and tribute, duty, and toll were paid to them.” (Ezra 4:20). He's pointing at Jerusalem's past under those kings. Tribute, duty and toll are part of what he says.

Stop is the word. The king says, “Now, therefore, issue an order for these men to stop…” (Ezra 4:21). The order goes to Rehum and Shimshai, and it holds until the king gives another order. One little word, and the whole job hits the brakes.

No follow-up letter shows up here. Once the king's letter is read, they “…went immediately to the Jews in Jerusalem and forcibly stopped them.” (Ezra 4:23). Immediately means they didn't wait. The text mentions no questions and no delay.
